title: Clean test history without hiding defects
objectives: Inspect DataFrame schema and missing values
relevance: A polished CI dashboard is misleading if ingestion silently drops flaky retries or imputes missing outcomes as success.

sections.title: Inspect before transforming
paragraphs: A DataFrame is a labeled table; each column is a Series. Start with head(), info(), dtypes, and isna().sum(). Read CSV with explicit types when identifiers have leading zeros. Parse timestamps with a defined timezone.
Selecting df["duration"] gives a Series; df[["duration"]] gives a DataFrame. Use .loc for explicit row and column selection. Copy a filtered slice before modifying it when isolation is required.
sections.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame([
    {"test": "login", "build": 1, "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5},
    {"test": "login", "build": 2, "status": "passed", "duration": None},
])
print(df.isna().sum())
print(df.loc[df["status"] == "failed", ["test", "build"]])

sections.title: Missing and duplicate records
paragraphs: A missing duration should remain unknown for latency analysis, not become zero. A missing status should be quarantined or counted separately. Preserve the denominator used in every metric.

Deduplicate by the ingestion identity, not merely by test name. Two executions of the same test in one build can be intentional retries. A stable key might include build_id, test_id, attempt, and environment. Keep raw data and document every cleaning decision.

sections.title: Engineering boundaries and independent checks
paragraphs: Missing data needs a domain interpretation before imputation. A missing duration may indicate a cancelled test; filling it with zero can make an outage look like a performance improvement. Preserve a missingness indicator and distinguish not-run from passed. Stable test IDs are safer join keys than display names that may be renamed.

Check duplicates on the intended identity, such as tenant, build and test, rather than dropping identical rows indiscriminately. A legitimate rerun has a different run ID and may be required to measure flakiness. Preserve raw records, clean in a reproducible function and count rejected or changed rows. Test malformed durations, duplicate identities and missing statuses, and verify that cleaning does not silently change the total population used for pass-rate metrics.

mistake: drop_duplicates("test") destroys historical runs and can erase flakiness.
takeaway: Data cleaning must preserve the events that explain quality problems.

title: Pass rates and flaky-test analysis
objectives: Keep run rate separate from test rate
Use mixed outcomes as evidence, not a verdict
relevance: A test that both passes and fails is a triage candidate. Confirm controlled conditions before labeling it flaky.

sections.title: Groupby makes the denominator explicit
paragraphs: Create a passed indicator and take its mean within each test group. This measures run-level pass rate. A test-level report answers a different question: how many distinct tests exhibit a behavior? Name the denominator in your report.

A mixed-outcome test has at least one pass and one fail in the observation window. Different code versions, environments, or test data can explain that pattern. Analyze repeated runs under comparable conditions before asserting nondeterministic flakiness.
sections.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"test": ["login", "login", "search"],
                   "status": ["failed", "passed", "passed"]})
df["passed"] = df["status"].eq("passed")
print(df.groupby("test")["passed"].mean())

sections.title: Build a CI health report
paragraphs: Aggregate counts, median duration, and p95 by module and build. Retain failed-first-attempt rate separately from eventual pass rate so retries cannot hide instability.

Sort by impact, not merely count: consider failure frequency, business criticality, added retry time, and reproducibility. Use pivot tables for build-by-module summaries and convert timestamps before resampling.

sections.title: Engineering boundaries and independent checks
paragraphs: A per-module pass rate needs the correct denominator. Excluding cancelled or missing-status rows may be a defensible policy, but report that exclusion; otherwise a module with many unexecuted tests can appear healthy. Weighted overall pass rate differs from the mean of module rates when modules have different numbers of runs.

Flakiness is not simply any test that ever failed. A candidate may show mixed pass/fail outcomes under comparable builds, but environment changes and product fixes can also explain the variation. Group by stable test identity, order by time and retain build context. Test all-pass, all-fail, mixed outcomes and one-run tests. Label the result a flaky-test candidate until the controlled reproduction establishes nondeterministic behavior.

mistake: A test passing after a retry is not evidence that its original failure was harmless.
takeaway: Report first-attempt outcomes and retries separately.

title: Joins, time windows, and regression signals
objectives: Compare duration trends within a test
relevance: Bad joins duplicate failures; uncontrolled comparisons make harmless dataset changes look like performance regressions.

sections.title: A join is a cardinality contract
paragraphs: Join executions to test metadata by stable test_id. validate="many_to_one" asserts that each metadata key appears once. A many-to-many join multiplies matching rows and inflates counts; inspect unmatched keys with indicator=True.
Use a left join to retain unknown tests for investigation. An inner join silently removes records with missing metadata. Group by environment and build when comparing performance.
sections.code:
# runs.merge(cases, on="test_id", how="left",
#            validate="many_to_one", indicator=True)
import pandas as pd
runs = pd.DataFrame({"test_id": [1,1,2], "duration": [2.,3.,1.]})
cases = pd.DataFrame({"test_id": [1,2], "module": ["auth","search"]})
print(runs.merge(cases, on="test_id", validate="many_to_one"))

sections.title: Time is an ordering constraint
paragraphs: Sort within a test by timestamp before shift() or rolling(). Use lagged features when predicting a future failure; a rolling window that includes the outcome leaks future information.
For a latency trend, compare median and tail within stable workloads and report sample sizes. A different mix of tests can change overall mean even when each test has unchanged latency.

sections.title: Engineering boundaries and independent checks
paragraphs: A many-to-many join multiplies rows. If a test appears twice in both tables, the joined result contains four combinations; a later mean or count can be wrong even though no exception occurred. Use validate='many_to_one' when enriching runs with a single testcase record, and inspect unmatched keys with an indicator column.

Parse timestamps with an explicit timezone and sort within the test group before calculating lagged duration features. Input row order is not a chronological guarantee. A future build's duration must not become a feature for an earlier prediction. Test duplicate enrichment keys, unmatched IDs, tied timestamps and timezone conversion. Compare row counts before and after the join and retain the reason for every intended change.

mistake: A duplicate metadata key can multiply execution rows without raising an error unless cardinality is checked.
takeaway: Assert join cardinality and align time before calculating trends.

objectives: Pivot tables, UTC time, and leakage-safe features
Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions

Build a CI health report with per-module counts, first-attempt pass rates, mixed-outcome candidates, UTC daily trends, and rejected records.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: A pivot table turns row observations into a labeled matrix after aggregation. Choose index, columns, values, and aggregation explicitly: module-by-build first-attempt failure rate differs from test-by-date mean duration. Missing cells mean no observation, not zero failures.

Parse timestamps to timezone-aware UTC before sorting or resampling. Daylight-saving changes and mixed local offsets can create ambiguous ordering. Keep categorical identifiers as categories only when their vocabulary and unknown-value policy are defined.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Use pd.to_datetime(..., utc=True), sort by test and timestamp, then group and shift to build lagged features. Merge metadata with validate="many_to_one". A rolling feature for prediction must use observations strictly before the predicted run.

Prefer vectorized transforms and map for straightforward substitutions; apply is useful for complex row logic but can be slower and conceal type changes. Inspect dtypes after transformations and keep raw evidence immutable.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A rolling window that includes the current outcome predicts itself. Filtering away tests with no recent runs can bias a report toward healthy frequently executed tests. Imputing absent modules with zero failure rate gives invented evidence.

Inspect the feature’s timestamp against the target timestamp. Check join multiplication, unmatched keys, and whether retries have been mistaken for separate test identities. Compare segment-level duration distributions before labeling an overall slowdown.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Build a CI health report with per-module counts, first-attempt pass rates, mixed-outcome candidates, UTC daily trends, and rejected records. Supply a small hand-calculated fixture to verify the pivot and lag behavior.

Feature engineering for the failure classifier should use only what was known when the run failed. Report the forecast horizon and validation split so another engineer can reproduce the apparent gain.

title: CI-health report: reruns, denominators and slow tests
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects ci-health report: reruns, denominators and slow tests with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. The deliverable is a CI-health artifact with policy, counts, failures, slow tests and data-quality notes.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: A useful CI-health report combines pass rate, failure frequency, slow-test summaries and data-quality warnings under one declared unit of analysis. A run-level pass rate counts every execution; a latest-result pass rate counts one result per test/build. Reruns make these different quantities, so name the policy in the report.
A flaky candidate needs mixed outcomes under comparable conditions, while a slow-test trend needs time order and context. Avoid turning a historical association into a confirmed product cause.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Validate stable test/build/run identities, sort reruns by run ID within a build and keep the declared latest result. Aggregate test count, failed count and pass rate from that selected table. Report slowest duration and missing duration count separately.

Use groupby for module summaries, pivot for a build-by-test status view and validated joins for ownership metadata. Keep an audit table of discarded reruns and malformed rows so the report's denominator is reproducible.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A rerun success hides an earlier failure if the report silently switches policies. Averaging module pass rates weights a tiny module as heavily as a large one. Missing-duration imputation makes cancelled tests look fast.
Test duplicate reruns, empty input, all-fail builds and missing durations. Compare aggregate counts with an independently computed tiny fixture before analyzing the full dataset.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
